docs.text: Driver AT25040B Driver ¶ A C++20 driver for the Microchip (formerly Atmel) AT25010B, AT25020B and AT25040B SPI serial EEPROMs. It checks that a chip really answers before trusting it, reads any range, writes page by page with the write enable latch, the write cycle and a read-back checked at every step, drives the WP pin and sets the block protection, on any MCU. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that brings the bus up, moves bytes and waits; it does the rest: the identity check, the instruction framing with A8, the page split, the write cycle, the WP pin and the checks that catch a dead or noisy bus. SPI serial EEPROM AT25010B / AT25020B / AT25040B Microchip (Atmel) Memory 128, 256 or 512 bytes; 8-byte pages; 1,000,000 write cycles, 100 years retention Interface SPI mode 0 or 3; 20 MHz from 4.5 V, 10 MHz from 2.5 V, 5 MHz from 1.8 V Write cycle Self-timed, 5 ms at most; no erase before a write Protection WP pin, write enable latch (WREN, WRDI), non-volatile block protection of a quarter, a half or all of the array Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V What you get ¶ One object per chip. AT25040B<YourPort> takes a reference to your port and does no I/O until EnsureInitialized() . See API guide . A probe that a dead bus cannot pass. docs.text: API guide ¶ The driver's API by task, with code that compiles: start and probe, read, write, protect, use it from a handler, and handle errors. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Microchip (Atmel) Atmel-8707 F: Write enable latch, WREN and WRDI: 6 Functional Description, Write Enable (WREN), Write Disable (WRDI), p. 8 Block write protection (BP1, BP0): 6 Functional Description, Write Status Register (WRSR), Table 6-4, p. 9 Sequential read and roll-over: 6 Functional Description, Read Sequence (READ), p. 9 Page write, the page wrap and the self-timed write cycle: 6 Functional Description, Write Sequence (WRITE), p. 9 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The shape of the API ¶ Group Calls Lifecycle EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() , Deinitialize() Configuration ApplyConfig() , GetConfig() , GetCapacityBytes() Memory Read() , Write() Status and protection ReadStatus() , GetBlockProtection() , SetBlockProtection() Diagnostics ReadRawStatus() , GetLastStatusByte() Free functions Validate() , CapacityBytes() , ProtectedFrom() , ToString() , GetDriverVersion() Every call that touches the chip returns Result<T> : check ok() (or the bool conversion) and read value , or read error . Result is [[nodiscard]] , so an unchecked call is a compiler warning. A failed call's value is T{} . Start and probe ¶ at25040b :: Error BringUp ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { // The one entry point: checks the chip on the first call, then returns Ok with no I/O. After a // failure the next call starts again from the beginning. const auto r = eeprom . EnsureInitialized (); if ( ! r ) { std :: printf ( "AT25040B: %s, status byte 0x%02X \n " , at25040b :: ToString ( r . error ), static_cast < unsigned > ( eeprom . GetLastStatusByte ())); } return r . error ; } The constructor stores the port and the configuration and does no I/O. EnsureInitialized() is the one way to start: it brings the bus up, parks WP and runs the identity check ( Contract ): the status read until idle and confirmed, then the write enable toggle. It writes nothing to the array. Once it has succeeded, EnsureInitialized() returns Ok at once with no I/O. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again. Every other call returns NotInitialized and sends nothing until then. GetLastStatusByte() keeps the last status byte read, by any call, for a log line: 0xFF, 0x05 and 0x00 say different things ( Troubleshooting ). ReadRawStatus() is the single-shot raw access: one RDSR, no wait, no retry, no check of the byte; RDSR has no side effect on the chip, so it is safe at any time, during a write cycle too (it then reads 0xFF). To probe again, for example on every attach of a removable module, Deinitialize() (WRDI, WP parked) and then EnsureInitialized() : at25040b :: Error Reprobe ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { // A handler probes again on every attach: Deinitialize() (WRDI, WP parked) makes the next // EnsureInitialized() run the identity check again. ( void ) eeprom . Deinitialize (); return eeprom . EnsureInitialized (). error ; } Read ¶ at25040b :: Error ReadImage ( Eeprom & eeprom , std :: array < uint8_t , 512 >& image ) { // Any length inside the array: the driver waits first if a write cycle is still running, then // splits it into 16-byte READs. Verify::ReadBack reads each twice and compares (BusNoise): use it // when the image carries no CRC of its own; the default reads each once. return eeprom . Read ( 0 , image , at25040b :: Verify :: ReadBack ). error ; } Read(address, out) reads out.size() bytes, any range inside the array; out is a std::span<uint8_t> , and a std::array or a C array converts to it. It first reads the status, and if a write cycle runs it waits for it (at most Config::write_timeout_us ): a busy chip ignores READ. Then it sends READs of at most 16 bytes ( kReadChunkBytes , why 16 ), with A8 recomputed for each, each read once. With Verify::ReadBack as the last argument it reads each chunk twice and compares ( BusNoise ); use it when the data carries no CRC of its own. The chip would roll over to address 0 at the top; the driver refuses a range past the end instead ( InvalidArgument ). After a failure the buffer is zeroed. Write ¶ Write(), step by step Figure description and sources Top to bottom, one card per step of Write(); a pill on a card names the error that step can return, and any step that sends a transfer also returns Bus when the transfer fails. The first two steps read the status (until no write cycle runs, confirmed by a second read) and refuse a range that overlaps the block-protected part before anything else is sent. WP is then released, if the port drives it. The band in the middle repeats once per 8-byte page: WREN and a status read that must show WEN = 1, the WRITE, a wait for the write cycle polled every kPollIntervalUs up to Config::write_timeout_us, a status that must show WEN = 0 again (still 1 means the chip ignored the WRITE), and only when the call passes Verify::ReadBack a read-back of the page. After the last page, or the first failure, WP is parked; a failure after WREN also sends WRDI. The steps and errors are read from writeRange(), writePage(), enableWrite(), finishWriteCycle(), waitIdle() and withWriteAccess() in src/at25040b.ipp. Drawn from: src/at25040b.ipp Write ; src/at25040b.ipp writeRange ; src/at25040b.ipp writePage ; src/at25040b.ipp enableWrite ; src/at25040b.ipp finishWriteCycle ; src/at25040b.ipp waitIdle ; src/at25040b.ipp withWriteAccess ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/write-path.py . at25040b :: Error WriteRecord ( Eeprom & eeprom , uint16_t address , std :: span < const uint8_t > data ) { // Split at 8-byte pages, WREN per page, wait for each write cycle; Verify::ReadBack reads each // page back (WriteMismatch). With a GpioSet() hook the driver raises WP for the call and parks // it low after. const auto r = eeprom . Write ( address , data , at25040b :: Verify :: ReadBack ); if ( r . error == at25040b :: Error :: BlockProtected ) { std :: printf ( "the range is block-protected: nothing was sent \n " ); } return r . error ; } Write(address, data) writes a std::span<const uint8_t> , any range inside the array. It refuses a range that overlaps the protected part before WREN ( BlockProtected ), raises WP through the port's GpioSet() , and then, per 8-byte page: WREN, a status read that must show WEN = 1 ( WriteProtected otherwise), the WRITE, a wait for the write cycle polled every 100 µs ( Timeout after Config::write_timeout_us ), a status that must show WEN = 0 again ( WriteMismatch when the chip ignored the WRITE), and with Verify::ReadBack as the last argument a read-back ( WriteMismatch ). WP is parked after, on success and failure. A 512-byte image is 64 pages, so 64 write cycles: up to 320 ms by the datasheet's maximum, usually less. The call blocks for all of it. After a failure, the pages before the failing one hold the new data (and were read back, with Verify::ReadBack ); the failing page may hold old, new or partly written data; nothing else changed. Writing the same data again is safe. Protect ¶ at25040b :: Error LockUpperHalf ( Eeprom & eeprom ) { // Non-volatile: one write cycle, then the level is read back. Nothing happens if it is set. if ( auto r = eeprom . SetBlockProtection ( at25040b :: BlockProtect :: UpperHalf ); ! r ) { return r . error ; // WriteProtected: WP low. WriteMismatch: the level did not take } const auto level = eeprom . GetBlockProtection (); return level ? at25040b :: Error :: Ok : level . error ; } SetBlockProtection(level) writes BP1:BP0 with WRSR (non-volatile, one write cycle) and reads the level back; when the chip already holds level it writes nothing. GetBlockProtection() reads it. The protected part is the top quarter, the top half or all of the array ( Hardware ). ReadStatus() returns one raw status read, decoded, without waiting; during a write cycle it says busy . Use it from a handler ¶ On a board, the driver sits under a handler that owns it, the port and the bus. The driver leaves to the handler what it cannot know: When to probe. Never from a static constructor or at boot: an unplugged module leaves MISO floating, and the bus may be shared. Construct the driver at boot if you like (it does no I/O), and call EnsureInitialized() from the attach path. On each attach, probe again with Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() . The shared bus. The driver takes no lock and never configures the bus. Take the bus lock in the handler (or the port) around each driver call, and pause other traffic on the bus for the call's duration. A read of the whole image is 34 transfers (66 with Verify::ReadBack ); a full write holds the bus through 64 write cycles, so release the lock between pages if another device cannot wait that long: split the write into page-sized calls. WP. Give the port a GpioSet() for the WP pin and let the driver drive it: high only for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, low after. Do not release WP in the handler around reads; nothing needs it. On a board with WP tied low, set Config::check_write_enable = false and accept the weaker check. Write policy. The driver writes when asked; which firmware may write, and when, is the handler's decision. Locks and time. The handler serialises the calls. A write blocks for its write cycles (about 5 ms per page at most) and polls the status every 100 µs through DelayUs() : implement DelayUs() with a sleep on an RTOS so the wait yields. Retries. The driver never retries. What to do on each error: Error In the probe In a read In a write NoDevice Module absent: report it, probe again on the next attach DeviceIdMismatch Not an AT25xxxB, MISO stuck low, or WP not reaching the chip: report, do not use BusNoise Contention on MISO: retry once, then report Retry the read once Retry the call once (rewriting is safe) Timeout The module was unplugged, or a cycle never ends: probe again Same WriteProtected WP is low: check the pin and the board BlockProtected Lower the protection first, or write elsewhere WriteMismatch Retry once; again means a worn or failing part Bus The port failed: check the bus, then probe again Same Same, then read back before trusting the data Pin The WP pin hook failed: check the GPIO, then probe again Same; WP may be left released, so read back Handle errors ¶ const char * Describe ( at25040b :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case at25040b :: Error :: NoDevice : return "nothing drives MISO: module unplugged, CS or VCC missing" ; case at25040b :: Error :: DeviceIdMismatch : return "the bus answers, but not like an AT25xxxB: MISO stuck or echoing, WP held low" ; case at25040b :: Error :: BusNoise : return "two reads disagreed: contention or noise on MISO, lower the clock" ; case at25040b :: Error :: WriteProtected : return "WP is low: release it, or the board ties it low" ; case at25040b :: Error :: WriteMismatch : return "the chip did not keep the write: retry once, then replace the part" ; default : return at25040b :: ToString ( e ); } } Signal Meaning What to do Error::NoDevice At start-up the status read 0xFF throughout: nothing drives MISO Module plugged in? CS, VCC, SO wiring; HOLD tied high Error::DeviceIdMismatch At start-up the bus answered, but not like an AT25xxxB 0x05: SI shorted to SO. 0x00: MISO stuck low, or WP not reaching pin 3 Error::BusNoise Two reads disagreed, or a status byte no chip sends Another device drives MISO; lower the clock; shorten the wires Error::Timeout After the start, the status stayed 0xFF longer than the timeout Module unplugged since the start, or a failing part: probe again Error::WriteProtected WREN did not set WEN WP low: the port's GpioSet() , the wiring, or a board that ties it low Error::BlockProtected The range is in the protected part; nothing was written SetBlockProtection(BlockProtect::None) first, if you mean it Error::WriteMismatch The chip did not keep a write, ignored a WRITE, or BP1:BP0 did not take Retry once; then suspect the part Error::Bus The port failed a transfer or the bus bring-up Check the port and the wiring; probe again Error::Pin The port's GpioSet() could not drive WP Check the WP GPIO and its configuration in the port Error::InvalidArgument A Config field or an argument is out of range; nothing was sent Fix the value ( Validate() , GetCapacityBytes() ) Error::NotInitialized EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded Call it Error::Crc , Error::Busy , Error::DeviceFault and Error::Unsupported belong to the shared base set but are never returned by this driver: the chip sends no CRC and reports no fault, every call waits for a write cycle instead of returning busy, and the driver has no optional feature. Every value, with the calls that return it, is on the Contract page. at25040b::ToString() names an error for a log. Next: Configuration .

CS, VCC, SO wiring; HOLD tied high Error::DeviceIdMismatch At start-up the bus answered, but not like an AT25xxxB 0x05: SI shorted to SO. 0x00: MISO stuck low, or WP not reaching pin 3 Error::BusNoise Two reads disagreed, or a status byte no chip sends Another device drives MISO; lower the clock; shorten the wires Error::Timeout After the start, the status stayed 0xFF longer than the timeout Module unplugged since the start, or a failing part: probe again Error::WriteProtected WREN did not set WEN WP low: the port's GpioSet() , the wiring, or a board that ties it low Error::BlockProtected The range is in the protected part; nothing was written SetBlockProtection(BlockProtect::None) first, if you mean it Error::WriteMismatch The chip did not keep a write, ignored a WRITE, or BP1:BP0 did not take Retry once; then suspect the part Error::Bus The port failed a transfer or the bus bring-up Check the port and the wiring; probe again Error::Pin The port's GpioSet() could not drive WP Check the WP GPIO and its configuration in the port Error::InvalidArgument A Config field or an argument is out of range; nothing was sent Fix the value ( Validate() , GetCapacityBytes() ) Error::NotInitialized EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded Call it Error::Crc , Error::Busy , Error::DeviceFault and Error::Unsupported belong to the shared base set but are never returned by this driver: the chip sends no CRC and reports no fault, every call waits for a write cycle instead of returning busy, and the driver has no optional feature. docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is built: three layers, one of them yours, and what happens in each when you read or write. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Microchip (Atmel) Atmel-8707 F: Instruction set and A8 in the opcode: 6 Functional Description, Table 6-1, p. 8 Sequential read and roll-over: 6 Functional Description, Read Sequence (READ), p. 9 Page write, the page wrap and the self-timed write cycle: 6 Functional Description, Write Sequence (WRITE), p. 9 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/at25040b.hpp public calls ; inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp SpiInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . A write is drawn on the API guide . Design choices ¶ CRTP, not virtual functions. The port is a template parameter constrained by the SpiPort concept, so every call is resolved at compile time and a missing hook is a compile error that names it. Optional hooks by named concepts. GpioSet and Log are detected by Has* concepts in one place, with their exact types and noexcept ; a hook that is declared with another signature is a compile error. A missing DelayUs() fails to compile, a missing GpioSet() leaves WP to the board, a missing Log() logs nothing. Spans, bounded at the bus helper. Read() and Write() take std::span ; the bus helper checks every length against its buffer before anything is sent (at compile time for a fixed extent), so no caller can overrun it. No I/O in the constructor. Construction cannot fail and clocks nothing, so the driver can be a static or a member of a handler built at boot, before the module is plugged in. Check the bus, not only the chip. The chip has no ID register and its idle status, 0x00, is also what a dead bus reads. So the start-up check uses behaviour a dead bus cannot fake (the write enable latch), status reads are confirmed, reads are read twice and writes read back. Wait inside the call. A write returns after its last write cycle, so the next call finds the chip ready and a handler holding a lock knows when the bus is free. One error type. Result<T> carries a value and an Error ; nothing throws and nothing returns a bare bool . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no printf . The driver is a header-only template with no mutable static state. Transfer buffers and the read chunk ¶ The port sees only the driver's two transfer buffers, tx_ and rx_ of detail::EepromBus : members of the driver object, so they live where the object lives (place it in DMA-capable memory if the port uses DMA), never on a caller's stack. Their size, kMaxTransferBytes = 18, is set by the read chunk, kReadChunkBytes = 16. The datasheet sets no limit on a READ, so 16 is a design choice: Chunk Buffers in the object Longest CS-low time at 5 MHz Command overhead 8 20 bytes 16 µs 20 % 16 36 bytes 29 µs 11 % 32 68 bytes 54 µs 6 % 512 (whole array) 1028 bytes 822 µs 0.4 % 16 keeps the buffers small, never holds a shared bus for long, is two whole pages (so a page read back is one READ) and costs little bus time. It is a compile-time constant, not a Config value: the buffers are sized from it and no value of it changes what the chip does. docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries under Breaking need source changes in code that used the affected API. [Unreleased] ¶ Changed ¶ The repository moved to kokeb-labs-drivers; URLs follow. The Hardware page draws the chip from the new docs/hardware.yml : the SOIC-8 pinout with each pin's port hook, the block diagram of Figure 3-1, the SPI wiring of Figure 5-1 with WP on a GPIO, and the pin and parts tables, every fact with its datasheet section and page. Values the datasheet does not give (the decoupling capacitor and the WP pull-down) are marked as not confirmed. The hand-written pin table is gone. The hardware-lessons-review , new-driver-from-template and verify skills follow the template, and tools/preflight.sh runs every local check before a push. The chip model's noise generator is parenthesised for the clang-tidy check that script now runs. The misra-review , cpp20-profile and new-driver-from-template skills and docs/repo-setup.md follow the template: reading the MISRA report, the known tool misfires, enumeration ranges without a sentinel, and the settings tool. [0.1.0] - 2026-11-09 ¶ Breaking ¶ Read() and Write() take a std::span instead of a pointer and a length: Read(uint16_t address, std::span<uint8_t> out, Verify) and Write(uint16_t address, std::span<const uint8_t> data, Verify) . Migration: Read(a, buf.data(), buf.size()) becomes Read(a, buf) (a std::array or a C array converts to the span), and Read(a, p, n) becomes Read(a, std::span{p, n}) . The null-pointer case is gone; an empty span is still InvalidArgument . A failed WP pin hook ( GpioSet() ) is reported as the new Error::Pin (21), the name the handbook gives a failed pin hook (KB-CPP-047), instead of Error::Bus , from EnsureInitialized() , Write() , SetBlockProtection() and Deinitialize() . Deinitialize() now returns Bus for a failed WRDI and Pin for a failed park, instead of Bus for both. When a step fails and parking WP fails too, any call returns Pin (WP may be left released) and logs it. A handler that mapped Bus to "check the pin" maps Pin now. The port concept checks every hook's exact types and noexcept : a Transfer() with a narrower length, a DelayUs() with a narrower parameter, or any hook without noexcept , is now a compile error. Error is [[nodiscard]] , so a discarded Validate() result warns. GetConfig() can no longer be called on a temporary driver ( const& overload only). Added ¶ The chip's SPI requirements as constexpr values in inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp (handbook KB-CPP-123): kSpiMode (0, and kSpiModeAlternate 3), kMsbFirst , kMaxClockHz , kMinCsHighNs , kCsSetupNs , kCsHoldNs , kDataSetupNs , kDataHoldNs , kContinuousWord , valid over the whole supply range, and BusTimingAt(supply_mv) with the faster limits from 2.5 V and 4.5 V (datasheet Table 4-3). The host, ESP32 and docs ports check their settings against them with static_assert ; the ESP32 port also checks its clock, mode and t_CSS at start, sets the CS hold time from the clock and drives CS high before the bus comes up (at most 5 MHz with that port). ReadRawStatus() : one RDSR, no wait, no retry, no check (handbook KB-CPP-129). Strict-dialect builds (KB-CPP20-001): CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF and -pedantic-errors in every folder that builds a target, the at25040b_header_checks target (each public header alone as ISO C++20, also in the Cortex-M cross-build) and examples/esp32/main/at25040b_cxx20_check.cpp inside ESP-IDF. tests/test_model.cpp : the chip model now carries its own register map and Table 6-4 from the datasheet and includes no driver header; the test cross-checks both maps at compile time (KB-TST-030). Compile-fail tests for a narrowed Transfer() length, a Transfer() without noexcept and a narrowed DelayUs() . From the template: the cpp20-profile , misra-review and hardware-lessons-review skills and the safety-reviewer agent. Changed ¶ MISRA C++:2023 conformance: std::fill replaces the discarded result of std::ranges::fill (Rule 0.1.2); the typed literals _u8 , _u16 and _u32 ( detail , out-of-range values do not compile) and explicit widening casts for constants and arguments of another type (Rule 7.0.6); both operands widened to uint32_t in a bitwise OR of two bytes (Rule 7.0.5); precedence-clarifying parentheses (Rule 8.0.1); loop bounds held in a const local, and the chunk and page loops that step their counter in the body written as while (Rule 9.5.1); default: break; in the ToString(Error) , CapacityBytes() and ProtectedFrom() switches, with -Wswitch-enum in the test flags so a new enumerator still warns (Rule 9.4.2); the .ipp include at the end of at25040b.hpp marked as deviation MD-CPP-009 (Rule 19.0.3). No change in behaviour. Follows the driver template's portable ownership: copyright belongs to The driver-at25040b authors ( LICENSE , every source header, driver.yml authors , the docs footer). tools/check_standalone.py runs in the Handbook source checks job and keeps the code and docs about this chip only. AGENTS.md follows the template's structure; the issue and PR templates ask for the board, MCU and port in one field. The port concepts match each hook's address against exactly one noexcept signature with detail::ExactHook<Port, Sig>::Take(&Port::Hook) instead of probing it with a converting detail::Exactly<T> : no conversion operator is left. A misdeclared hook is still a compile error. kAlwaysFalse takes a class and the enumeration helpers an enumeration ( ClassType , Enumeration ), each with a compile-fail test. The bus helper checks every length against its buffer before it sends anything: a READ of 1 to 16 bytes, a WRITE of 1 to 8 bytes inside one page, an address up to A8 ( InvalidArgument otherwise; at compile time for a fixed-size span). The transfer buffers are members of the driver object, so the port never sees a caller's or a stack buffer (handbook KB-HW-019). The receive buffer is preset to MISO's idle level (0xFF) before each READ, so a port that reports success without filling it can never hand back an earlier transfer's bytes. The driver object grows by 36 bytes; the hot path is unchanged apart from these comparisons and buffer fills. The read chunk, kReadChunkBytes = 16, now states its design reason (buffer size, longest CS-low time on a shared bus, command overhead, two whole pages); see the Architecture page. Include guards instead of #pragma once in every header (KB-CPP-019); uint32_t casts before every ~ , << , | , & and ^ on register values (KB-CPP20-021); BP1:BP0 through a typed Field ; the toggle error and the BP encoders are free constexpr functions with static_assert s; withWriteAccess() is constrained; enumerator checks through detail::IsEnumerator ; ToString() is a switch over every enumerator. Template sync to a4a1056 : _config/.clang-tidy , ci-repo-checks.yml (handbook source checks pinned), skills. Added ¶ First version of the driver for the Microchip (Atmel) AT25010B, AT25020B and AT25040B SPI serial EEPROMs, written on the Kokeb Labs driver template. at25040b::AT25040B<Port> with the configuration in the constructor (no I/O) and one start-up call, EnsureInitialized() : the status read until idle and confirmed by a second read, then the write enable latch toggled (WREN, WEN = 1, WRDI, WEN = 0) with nothing programmed, so a floating, stuck-low or echoing MISO fails the check. Config::check_write_enable = false falls back to reading the first 8 bytes twice, for boards with WP tied low. Deinitialize() (WRDI, WP parked) followed by EnsureInitialized() probes again. Read() of any range in 16-byte transfers, each read twice and compared ( Config::verify_reads ); Write() of any range split at 8-byte pages, with WREN and a WEN check per page, the write cycle waited for ( Config::write_timeout_us , default 10 ms), the latch checked again and each page read back ( Config::verify_writes ). A range in the block-protected part is refused before anything is sent. SetBlockProtection() , GetBlockProtection() , ReadStatus() , GetLastStatusByte() ; Config::variant for the three sizes, with A8 in the opcode on the AT25040B. The optional GpioSet(CtrlPin::WriteProtect, ...) port hook: WP is released only for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, and parked after, on success and failure. Chip-specific errors from 16: NoDevice , BusNoise , WriteProtected , BlockProtected , WriteMismatch . Host tests over a protocol model of the three parts with the bus and board faults the datasheet's pin descriptions allow, every transfer and WP pin write of every operation failed in turn, a libFuzzer target with corpus replay, the host and ESP32 examples, three figures drawn from the code. Not verified on hardware; the bench checks are in docs/limitations.md . Changed ¶ CI runs fewer jobs, from the driver template: the host tests build GCC and Clang in one job; DCO, the org standard, Markdown and YAML lint, the handbook rules, template drift and cppcheck are steps of one Repository checks job ( ci-repo-checks.yml , replacing ci-handbook.yml , ci-cpp-analysis.yml , ci-markdown-lint.yml and ci-yaml-lint.yml ); cross-compile and host quality use ci-tools' one-job layouts. No check is dropped. The workflows have no manual ( workflow_dispatch ) trigger any more. Read and write verification is opt-in and chosen per call: Read() and Write() take a last argument, at25040b::Verify ( None , the default, or ReadBack ). By default Read() reads each 16-byte chunk once and Write() reads no page back, so a call sends only what the datasheet needs plus the status reads that keep it off a busy chip. Verify::ReadBack restores the double read ( BusNoise ) and the per-page read-back ( WriteMismatch ). Config::verify_reads , Config::verify_writes and their Kconfig options CONFIG_AT25040B_SKIP_READ_VERIFY and CONFIG_AT25040B_SKIP_WRITE_VERIFY are removed. Config::check_write_enable stays on by default: it runs once, in EnsureInitialized() , never on the Read() and Write() path.

Fields ¶ The chip has no setting to configure: its only one, the block protection, is non-volatile and set with SetBlockProtection() . Config describes the board instead: which part is fitted, how WP is wired, and whether the start-up identity check runs. Config{} is an AT25040B with WP driven by the port (or tied high) and the identity check on. Read and write verification is not a Config field: each call chooses it ( below ). Field Default Range What it does variant Variant::At25040b At25010b , At25020b , At25040b The fitted part: 128, 256 or 512 bytes. Every address is checked against it; A8 is used only on the AT25040B check_write_enable true The write enable toggle at start-up ( Contract ). Runs once, in EnsureInitialized() , never on the Read() and Write() path; it is what tells a dead bus from a chip. Turn it off only when WP is tied low write_timeout_us 10000 5000 to 1000000 Longest wait for a write cycle, in µs. t WC is 5 ms at most (Table 4-3) The chip cannot tell its size: a wrong variant either wastes the top of a larger part or, on a smaller part, lets an address alias the start of the array. EnsureInitialized (). error ; } Verification per call ¶ Read() and Write() take a last argument, at25040b::Verify , default Verify::None : the call sends only what the datasheet needs, plus the status reads that keep it off a busy chip. docs.text: Contract ¶ What the AT25040B driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. A change to anything here is a breaking change, listed under Breaking in the changelog . Datasheet sections this page relies on From Microchip (Atmel) Atmel-8707 F: Write enable latch, WREN and WRDI: 6 Functional Description, Write Enable (WREN), Write Disable (WRDI), p. 8 Status register, RDY and the all-ones status of a write cycle: 6 Functional Description, Tables 6-2 and 6-3, p. 8 Page write, the page wrap and the self-timed write cycle: 6 Functional Description, Write Sequence (WRITE), p. 9 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , does no I/O and cannot fail. No call clocks the bus before EnsureInitialized() , so the driver can be constructed statically even where MISO may float. EnsureInitialized() runs the identity check below and nothing else; it never sends WRITE or WRSR. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised, and the next call starts again. Every call that touches the chip returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds and sends nothing. No call starts the chip as a side effect. Every port failure propagates: a failed transfer as Error::Bus , a failed WP pin write as Error::Pin . When a step fails and parking WP fails too, the call returns Pin (WP may be left released) and logs both. A failed Read() leaves its buffer zeroed, never partial data. Before each array access and after each write the driver reads the status until no write cycle runs (at most Config::write_timeout_us ), and an idle status counts only when a second read gives the same byte. It never sends an instruction a busy chip would ignore. Write() never sends a WRITE that crosses a page, never writes outside the requested range, and refuses a range in the block-protected part before it sends WREN. It returns only after the last write cycle has ended. Read() and Write() send only what the datasheet needs, plus the status reads above, unless the call asks for more. Verification is chosen per call: with Verify::ReadBack , one corrupted transfer never makes Read() return wrong bytes with Ok , and never makes Write() return Ok for bytes the chip does not hold. With Verify::None , the default, a corrupted READ reaches the caller (check a CRC over the data), and a WRITE the chip ignored is still caught by the WEN check after its write cycle. WP is high only during a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, and parked low after each of them, on success and on failure. A failure after WREN sends WRDI, so the latch is not left set. SetBlockProtection() is the only call that sends WRSR, and only when the level changes. A missing DelayUs() is a compile error; a missing GpioSet() leaves WP to the board; a missing Log() logs nothing. A misdeclared hook is a compile error. The driver never retries a call. Retries are the caller's choice ( API guide ). The identity check ¶ The identity check, and what a broken bus looks like Figure description and sources The left column is the start-up as the driver runs it, top to bottom; a pill names the error a step returns, and any step that sends a transfer also returns Bus when it fails. The status is read until it is not busy, for at most Config::write_timeout_us, and an idle status counts only when a second read gives the same byte. With Config::check_write_enable (the default) WP is released, the latch cleared first if it was set, then WREN must show WEN = 1 and WRDI WEN = 0, and WP is parked again; nothing is programmed. Without it, for a board whose WP is tied low, the first kIdentityReadBytes are read twice and must match, a weaker test. The right column lists the bus and board faults the host tests put on the chip model, each with the status byte the driver saw and the error EnsureInitialized() returned, read from the test cases in tests/test_at25040b.cpp. The steps come from initialize(), checkWriteEnableToggle(), checkStableHead() and waitIdle() in src/at25040b.ipp. Drawn from: src/at25040b.ipp initialize ; src/at25040b.ipp checkWriteEnableToggle ; src/at25040b.ipp checkStableHead ; src/at25040b.ipp waitIdle ; tests/test_at25040b.cpp start-up fault tests ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/identity-check.py . The AT25xxxB family has no ID register, so EnsureInitialized() checks behaviour the datasheet guarantees, strongest test first: The status, read until idle and confirmed. Bits 7 to 4 read 0 when no write cycle runs, and every bit reads 1 during one (Table 6-3). The driver reads the status until it is not 0xFF (a write cycle may still run after an MCU reset), for at most Config::write_timeout_us , then once more: both reads must be the same idle status. 0xFF throughout is NoDevice (MISO floating high); 0x05 (the RDSR opcode echoed from MOSI) or any byte with bits 7 to 4 or RDY set is DeviceIdMismatch ; two different idle bytes are BusNoise . The write enable latch follows WREN and WRDI ( Config::check_write_enable , the default). WP is released, the latch cleared first if it was already set, then WREN must make WEN read 1 and WRDI must make it read 0, and WP is parked again. Nothing is programmed. A MISO stuck low reads 0x00, which passes step 1 like an idle chip, but it can never show WEN = 1: WEN is set only by a WREN the chip received with WP high (section 6, "Write Enable"; Table 6-2), so it proves that a chip, not a line, answers. Without step 2 , for a board whose WP pin is tied low (the chip then never sets WEN), the first kIdentityReadBytes (8) are read twice and must match ( BusNoise otherwise). This is weaker: a dead bus with MISO stuck low passes it. The check cannot tell the part's size, so Config::variant is trusted. Depends on ¶ Dependency Version Why A C++20 compiler GCC 10, Clang 13 or later Concepts constrain the port CMake 3.16 or later Generates at25040b_version.h Your port The bus, a delay, optionally the WP pin and logging ( Porting ) Nothing else: no RTOS, no SDK, no other repository of the org. Threading ¶ The driver is not thread-safe and takes no lock. Use each driver object from one task at a time, or guard every call on it with one mutex; the layer that owns the driver owns that lock, and the bus lock when several chips share a bus. Nothing may run in an ISR: every call can block for transfers and, for a write, for the write cycles (about 5 ms per page at most, Config::write_timeout_us per page in the worst case). Separate objects share no state. Timing ¶ Call Transfers Waits EnsureInitialized() 6 (8 if the latch was set) Only while a write cycle runs Read() of n bytes 2 + ceil(n / 16); 2 + 2 x ceil(n / 16) with Verify::ReadBack Only while a write cycle runs Write() of p pages 2 + 5 x p, plus status polls; 2 + 6 x p with Verify::ReadBack Each write cycle, polled every 100 µs SetBlockProtection() 7, plus status polls (2 when the level is already set) One write cycle GetBlockProtection() , ReadStatus() 2, 1 GetBlockProtection() only while a cycle runs With Verify::None the transfers beyond the datasheet's own sequence are: the second, confirming status read before a Read() or Write() and after each write cycle (one corrupted read must not let the driver send a READ or WREN to a busy chip, which ignores it: found by the fuzzer), and the status read after each WREN (WEN = 1, so WP low is WriteProtected before a WRITE is sent). The WEN = 0 check after a write cycle reuses the last status read. Config::check_write_enable adds nothing to Read() or Write() : it runs once, in EnsureInitialized() . Why the status read after each WREN is not opt-in. The datasheet requires a WREN before every WRITE, and the latch clears at the end of each write cycle, so a WREN per page is part of the datasheet's sequence. The status read after it is one more short transfer. Each page then waits for its self-timed write cycle, up to 5 ms, which makes that read a small fraction of the page's time. In return a chip that did not take the WREN (WP held low, a broken MOSI) is reported as WriteProtected before the WRITE is sent, instead of a write that silently did nothing. EEPROM writes are not a timing-critical path, so this check stays on every page. Opt-in verification ( Verify::ReadBack ) is for checks that cost a read of the data itself. Errors ¶ at25040b::Error inside at25040b::Result<T> . Values 0 to 9 are the shared base set; this driver returns six of them, plus six chip-specific values. Error Value Returned when Ok 0 The call succeeded NotInitialized 1 EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded, or Deinitialize() ran since InvalidArgument 2 A Config field fails Validate() , an address range leaves the array, an empty range, or a block-protection level that is not one; nothing was sent Bus 3 A transfer, or the port's bus bring-up, failed Timeout 4 After the start, the status read busy for longer than Config::write_timeout_us : a write cycle that does not end, or the module was unplugged since DeviceIdMismatch 5 At start-up, a status byte that is neither idle nor busy, or the latch did not follow WREN and WRDI Crc 6 Never returned: the chip sends no CRC Busy 7 Never returned: every call waits for a running write cycle instead DeviceFault 8 Never returned: the chip reports no faults Unsupported 9 Never returned: the driver has no optional feature NoDevice 16 At start-up, the status read 0xFF for the whole timeout: nothing drives MISO BusNoise 17 Two reads of the same thing differed, or after the start a status byte was neither idle nor busy WriteProtected 18 WREN did not set WEN: WP is low, or the WREN frame was lost; nothing was written BlockProtected 19 The range lies in the block-protected part; only the status was read WriteMismatch 20 The read-back differed, the latch was still set after a WRITE (the chip ignored it), or BP1:BP0 did not take Pin 21 The port's GpioSet() could not release or park WP (handbook KB-CPP-047) The API guide says what to do about each. Memory ¶ No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no std::string , no printf and no static mutable state. A driver object holds a reference to the port, its two 18-byte transfer buffers (the only memory the port sees), a Config , the last status byte and a flag: about 56 bytes on a 32-bit MCU. Stack use is small and fixed: a 16-byte compare buffer in Read() with Verify::ReadBack , an 8-byte one in Write() . Platform ¶ Platform-free: the same code runs on any target with a C++20 compiler, including the host tests. The ESP-IDF port in examples/esp32 is an example, not part of the driver. Deviations from the standard ¶ Rule Deviation Why A chip-ID check at start-up Replaced by the behaviour check above The chip has no ID register A reset at start-up None The chip has no reset; it powers up with the latch clear (section 6, "Write Enable") Config{} equals the chip's reset state Config describes the board (variant, WP wiring, checks), not chip registers The only setting, BP1:BP0, is non-volatile and is never written by EnsureInitialized()

docs.text: The driver is not thread-safe and takes no lock. Use each driver object from one task at a time, or guard every call on it with one mutex; the layer that owns the driver owns that lock, and the bus lock when several chips share a bus. Nothing may run in an ISR: every call can block for transfers and, for a write, for the write cycles (about 5 ms per page at most, Config::write_timeout_us per page in the worst case). Separate objects share no state.

docs.text: Call Transfers Waits EnsureInitialized() 6 (8 if the latch was set) Only while a write cycle runs Read() of n bytes 2 + ceil(n / 16); 2 + 2 x ceil(n / 16) with Verify::ReadBack Only while a write cycle runs Write() of p pages 2 + 5 x p, plus status polls; 2 + 6 x p with Verify::ReadBack Each write cycle, polled every 100 µs SetBlockProtection() 7, plus status polls (2 when the level is already set) One write cycle GetBlockProtection() , ReadStatus() 2, 1 GetBlockProtection() only while a cycle runs With Verify::None the transfers beyond the datasheet's own sequence are: the second, confirming status read before a Read() or Write() and after each write cycle (one corrupted read must not let the driver send a READ or WREN to a busy chip, which ignores it: found by the fuzzer), and the status read after each WREN (WEN = 1, so WP low is WriteProtected before a WRITE is sent). The WEN = 0 check after a write cycle reuses the last status read. Config::check_write_enable adds nothing to Read() or Write() : it runs once, in EnsureInitialized() . Why the status read after each WREN is not opt-in. The datasheet requires a WREN before every WRITE, and the latch clears at the end of each write cycle, so a WREN per page is part of the datasheet's sequence. The status read after it is one more short transfer. Each page then waits for its self-timed write cycle, up to 5 ms, which makes that read a small fraction of the page's time. In return a chip that did not take the WREN (WP held low, a broken MOSI) is reported as WriteProtected before the WRITE is sent, instead of a write that silently did nothing. EEPROM writes are not a timing-critical path, so this check stays on every page. Opt-in verification ( Verify::ReadBack ) is for checks that cost a read of the data itself.

docs.text: No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no std::string , no printf and no static mutable state. A driver object holds a reference to the port, its two 18-byte transfer buffers (the only memory the port sees), a Config , the last status byte and a flag: about 56 bytes on a 32-bit MCU. Stack use is small and fixed: a 16-byte compare buffer in Read() with Verify::ReadBack , an 8-byte one in Write() .

HOLD. HOLD low while SCK is low pauses the chip and leaves SO in high impedance (section 5). Strapped to CS, it is low for every instruction, so every status read returns MISO's pull-up level: the driver sees no chip ( NoDevice ). WP. With WP low the chip ignores WREN, so no write starts; WRDI still works. WP going low while CS is low interrupts a write that has not started its cycle; once the cycle runs, WP has no effect (section 5). The driver raises WP (through GpioSet() ) only for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, and parks it low after, whatever happened. Inside the chip ¶ Inside the AT25040B Figure description and sources The AT25040B's function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp . The circuit adds what the driver and the chip need around them: WP on a GPIO with a pull-down that keeps writes blocked until the MCU drives it, HOLD tied to VCC, and a decoupling capacitor. The datasheet gives no power-up time. Instructions ¶ Six instructions, one transfer each Figure description and sources Each row is one transfer, CS low from the first byte to the last, drawn left to right in the order the bytes are clocked; the top line of a byte is what the driver sends on MOSI, the bottom line what it keeps from MISO. Every opcode is 0000 followed by four bits, written out in binary. For READ and WRITE, bit 3 of the opcode carries address bit A8 on the AT25040B and the next byte holds A7 to A0; the driver sets A8 for addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF and never on the smaller parts. RDSR returns the status in its second byte; READ returns data from the third byte on, up to kReadChunkBytes per transfer; WRITE carries 1 to kPageSizeBytes data bytes inside one page. WREN, WRDI, WRSR and WRITE need no reply, and the driver passes no receive buffer for them. The opcodes come from inc/at25040b_registers.hpp and the byte layouts from detail::EepromBus in inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp. Drawn from: inc/at25040b_registers.hpp opcodes ; inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp detail::EepromBus ; inc/at25040b_types.hpp kReadChunkBytes ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/instruction-frames.py . Instruction Opcode What it does Used by WREN 0x06 Sets the write enable latch; WP must be high Every write, SetBlockProtection() , the identity check WRDI 0x04 Clears the latch, whatever WP does The identity check, Deinitialize() , after a failed write RDSR 0x05 Reads the status; the only instruction a busy chip answers Every call WRSR 0x01 Writes BP1 and BP0: non-volatile, takes a write cycle SetBlockProtection() READ 0x03 , 0x0B with A8 Address byte, then data; the address counts up and rolls over at the top Read() , write verification WRITE 0x02 , 0x0A with A8 Address byte, then 1 to 8 data bytes in one page Write() Bit 3 of READ and WRITE carries address bit A8 on the AT25040B only (Table 6-1, note 1); on the smaller parts the driver never sets it, because it checks every address against the configured variant. An invalid opcode leaves SO in high impedance until the next CS falling edge (section 5). Status register ¶ Bit Name Meaning 0 RDY 1 while a write cycle runs 1 WEN 1 when the write enable latch is set 2 BP0 Block protection, low bit 3 BP1 Block protection, high bit 7 to 4 0 when no write cycle runs During a write cycle every bit reads 1 (Table 6-3), so a busy chip returns 0xFF. An idle chip returns 0000 BBW0 . Any other byte (0x05, for example) is not a status: the driver treats it as DeviceIdMismatch at start-up and BusNoise after. A floating-high MISO also reads 0xFF, which is why the driver waits at most Config::write_timeout_us before calling it no chip. Writes and the write cycle ¶ A WRITE needs WP high and the latch set by WREN first; the chip ignores it otherwise and returns to standby when CS goes high (section 6, "Write Sequence"). Inside one WRITE only the three low address bits count up: a ninth byte wraps to the start of the page and overwrites it. The write cycle starts when CS goes high and ends with the latch cleared. During it the chip ignores every instruction except RDSR. The driver therefore splits a write at 8-byte page boundaries, sends WREN before each page, checks that WEN reads 1, waits for the cycle, checks that WEN reads 0 again and reads the page back. Block protection ¶ Level BP1 BP0 AT25010B AT25020B AT25040B None 00 none none none UpperQuarter 01 0x60 to 0x7F 0xC0 to 0xFF 0x180 to 0x1FF UpperHalf 10 0x40 to 0x7F 0x80 to 0xFF 0x100 to 0x1FF All 11 0x00 to 0x7F 0x00 to 0xFF 0x000 to 0x1FF BP1 and BP0 are non-volatile: they need WREN, take a write cycle and survive power-off like the array (section 6, "Write Status Register", Table 6-4). A new part reads level None . The driver refuses a write into a protected range ( BlockProtected ) before it sends WREN. Power ¶ Quantity Value VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V; the clock limit depends on it Read or write current at 5 V 10 mA max at 20 MHz, 3 mA max at 1 MHz Standby current (CS high) 0.5 µA max at 1.8 V, 1 µA at 2.5 V, 3.5 µA at 5 V Temperature -40 °C to +85 °C (industrial grade) The inputs need V IH of at least 0.7 x VCC, so run the chip from the MCU's I/O supply. The datasheet gives no decoupling value; 100 nF next to pin 8, as in the circuit above, is the usual choice. Variants ¶ Part Size Marking code AT25010B 128 x 8 51B AT25020B 256 x 8 52B AT25040B 512 x 8, A8 in the opcode 54B The chip cannot report its size: set Config::variant to the fitted part. On a smaller part an address past its size would alias the start of the array; the driver refuses it with InvalidArgument . Sharing the bus ¶ SO is high impedance while CS is high, so the chip can share SCK, MOSI and MISO with other devices on their own chip selects. docs.text: Six instructions, one transfer each Figure description and sources Each row is one transfer, CS low from the first byte to the last, drawn left to right in the order the bytes are clocked; the top line of a byte is what the driver sends on MOSI, the bottom line what it keeps from MISO. Every opcode is 0000 followed by four bits, written out in binary. For READ and WRITE, bit 3 of the opcode carries address bit A8 on the AT25040B and the next byte holds A7 to A0; the driver sets A8 for addresses 0x100 to 0x1FF and never on the smaller parts. RDSR returns the status in its second byte; READ returns data from the third byte on, up to kReadChunkBytes per transfer; WRITE carries 1 to kPageSizeBytes data bytes inside one page. WREN, WRDI, WRSR and WRITE need no reply, and the driver passes no receive buffer for them. The opcodes come from inc/at25040b_registers.hpp and the byte layouts from detail::EepromBus in inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp. Drawn from: inc/at25040b_registers.hpp opcodes ; inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp detail::EepromBus ; inc/at25040b_types.hpp kReadChunkBytes ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/instruction-frames.py . Instruction Opcode What it does Used by WREN 0x06 Sets the write enable latch; WP must be high Every write, SetBlockProtection() , the identity check WRDI 0x04 Clears the latch, whatever WP does The identity check, Deinitialize() , after a failed write RDSR 0x05 Reads the status; the only instruction a busy chip answers Every call WRSR 0x01 Writes BP1 and BP0: non-volatile, takes a write cycle SetBlockProtection() READ 0x03 , 0x0B with A8 Address byte, then data; the address counts up and rolls over at the top Read() , write verification WRITE 0x02 , 0x0A with A8 Address byte, then 1 to 8 data bytes in one page Write() Bit 3 of READ and WRITE carries address bit A8 on the AT25040B only (Table 6-1, note 1); on the smaller parts the driver never sets it, because it checks every address against the configured variant. An invalid opcode leaves SO in high impedance until the next CS falling edge (section 5).

docs.text: Bit Name Meaning 0 RDY 1 while a write cycle runs 1 WEN 1 when the write enable latch is set 2 BP0 Block protection, low bit 3 BP1 Block protection, high bit 7 to 4 0 when no write cycle runs During a write cycle every bit reads 1 (Table 6-3), so a busy chip returns 0xFF. An idle chip returns 0000 BBW0 . Any other byte (0x05, for example) is not a status: the driver treats it as DeviceIdMismatch at start-up and BusNoise after. A floating-high MISO also reads 0xFF, which is why the driver waits at most Config::write_timeout_us before calling it no chip.
docs.title: Status register

docs.text: A WRITE needs WP high and the latch set by WREN first; the chip ignores it otherwise and returns to standby when CS goes high (section 6, "Write Sequence"). Inside one WRITE only the three low address bits count up: a ninth byte wraps to the start of the page and overwrites it. The write cycle starts when CS goes high and ends with the latch cleared. During it the chip ignores every instruction except RDSR. The driver therefore splits a write at 8-byte page boundaries, sends WREN before each page, checks that WEN reads 1, waits for the cycle, checks that WEN reads 0 again and reads the page back.

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( at25040b_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-at25040b.git external/driver-at25040b git submodule update --init external/driver-at25040b Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-at25040b ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE at25040b::at25040b ) at25040b::at25040b is an alias of the at25040b INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect AT25040B_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver AT25040B_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-at25040b -B build-at25040b cmake --install build-at25040b --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( at25040b 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE at25040b::at25040b ) The target is at25040b::at25040b in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated at25040b_version.h go to include/at25040b/inc/ , the template implementation to include/at25040b/src/at25040b.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-at25040b) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-at25040b (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-at25040b.git components/at25040b at25040b (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml at25040b (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : at25040b : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-at25040b.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES at25040b (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/at25040b_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into at25040b_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = at25040b :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: Status and limitations ¶ What this driver has and has not been shown to do, so you can decide whether it is ready for your use. Status ¶ Version 0.1.0, not released On hardware Not verified on hardware. No board has run this driver yet Tested against A protocol model of the three parts ( Testing and CI ), a fuzzer and the quality gates Assurance level high (Kokeb Labs handbook): not qualified for use in a safety function Bus faults the design handles ¶ The chip gives the driver little to prove that it is there: it has no ID register, and its idle status is 0x00 (bits 7 to 4 read 0 outside a write cycle, Table 6-3). When no chip drives it, SO is in high impedance (section 5, "Chip Select"), so MISO carries whatever the board's pull, a short or a loop-back puts on it. The driver is built so that none of these can pass for a chip: A MISO pulled or stuck low reads 0x00, an idle status. So the start-up check does not stop at the status: it toggles the write enable latch. WEN is set only by a WREN the chip received with WP held high and cleared by WRDI (section 6, "Write Enable (WREN)", "Write Disable (WRDI)"; Table 6-2), which a stuck line cannot follow ( Contract ). A Read() with Verify::ReadBack reads every chunk twice. The model has the fault ( Miso::StuckLow ); the tests and the fuzzer cover it. 0xFF is a busy chip before it is an absent one. Every status bit reads 1 during a write cycle (Table 6-3), and a cycle started before an MCU reset still runs for up to t WC (5 ms, Table 4-3). The driver therefore waits for up to Config::write_timeout_us before it reports NoDevice , and it tests for the busy byte before it looks at RDY. Probe on attach, not at boot. An unplugged module leaves MISO to its pull, so a probe at boot can only fail. The constructor does no I/O and nothing but EnsureInitialized() probes, so a handler probes when it knows the module is there. HOLD strapped to CS makes the status read fail. HOLD low while SCK is low pauses the chip and keeps SO in high impedance (section 5, "Hold"), so a HOLD tied to CS is low for every instruction. Tie HOLD high; the driver reports the strapped case as NoDevice , and the model has the fault ( hold_tied_to_cs ). WP stays low except while it is needed. WP low inhibits every write, and WP going low while CS is low interrupts a write that has not started its cycle (section 5, "Write Protect"). The driver releases WP only for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check (WREN needs WP high), and parks it after each, on failure too. What the model cannot show ¶ The model is written from the datasheet, by the same reading as the driver. It cannot show: whether WEN clears at the end of a WRSR cycle. The datasheet says so for WRITE; the driver does not depend on it for WRSR (it reads BP1:BP0 back and sends WRDI if WEN is still set); what a real chip does with a WRITE into a protected range (the model ignores it; the driver never sends one); electrical behaviour: the clock limits, CS timing, a slow MISO edge, the real write cycle time (the model uses 3 ms); what a partly clocked WRITE does when a transfer fails half way: the driver treats that page as unknown. Before you depend on it ¶ Run these on your board behind the handler, and record the result below: Module plugged: EnsureInitialized() returns Ok ; GetLastStatusByte() is 0x00 (or 0x0C etc. with block protection set). Module unplugged: NoDevice (status 0xFF) or DeviceIdMismatch (status 0x00), never Ok . WP held low by hand, module plugged: DeviceIdMismatch with check_write_enable on. Read the whole 512-byte image twice with Read(0, image, Verify::ReadBack) ( image a std::array<uint8_t, 512> ): identical both times. Once more with the default ( Verify::None ): the same bytes. On a scrap module, the whole array: Write(0, image, Verify::ReadBack) returns Ok in about 64 write cycles; read it back with Verify::ReadBack . Watch WP on a scope or logic analyser during the probe and the write: high only during WREN/WRDI and the write. In SPI mode 3, write a page and read it back; on a logic analyser, CS must rise while SCK is low after the last data bit (section 6, "Write Sequence"). At the port's highest clock, measure t CSS , t CSH and t CS against Table 4-3 for the board's supply. docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the port. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Microchip (Atmel) Atmel-8707 F: SPI clock, CS timing and the write cycle time: 4.3 AC Characteristics, Table 4-3, p. 5 SPI modes, invalid opcodes, HOLD and the WP pin: 5 Serial Interface Description, p. 6 Instruction timing: 7 Timing Diagrams, Figures 7-1 to 7-8, p. 10 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on a class you derive from at25040b::SpiInterface<Self> (in inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp ). The base uses CRTP and declares no hook itself; the driver template is constrained by the at25040b::SpiPort concept, so calls are resolved at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error at the point of use. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the bus up on the first call; return true at once afterwards. false makes the driver's EnsureInitialized() return Bus bool Transfer(const uint8_t* tx, uint8_t* rx, std::size_t len) noexcept yes One full-duplex transfer of len bytes (1 to 18) with CS low for all of them and high after. rx is nullptr when the driver needs no reply. false on any bus error void DelayUs(uint32_t us) noexcept yes Wait at least us microseconds: the status polls during a write cycle, 100 µs each bool GpioSet(CtrlPin, GpioSignal) noexcept no Drive WP ( CtrlPin::WriteProtect ): ACTIVE is pin low (protected), INACTIVE pin high; false if the pin write failed, which the driver returns as Error::Pin void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) noexcept no Print one line; message is plain text, never a format string The port ¶ my_port.hpp // Your board's bus settings, checked against what the chip needs (handbook KB-CPP-123). inline constexpr uint32_t kMySupplyMv = 3300 ; // lowest VCC the board sees inline constexpr uint32_t kMyClockHz = 8'000'000 ; // what platform_spi_init() programs inline constexpr uint8_t kMySpiMode = 0 ; // CPOL 0, CPHA 0 inline constexpr bool kMyMsbFirst = true ; // the SDK's bit order inline constexpr uint32_t kMyCsGapNs = 1000 ; // CS high between two transfers, as measured static_assert ( kMyClockHz <= at25040b :: BusTimingAt ( kMySupplyMv ). max_clock_hz , "SCK above f_SCK max at this supply (Table 4-3)" ); static_assert ( kMySpiMode == at25040b :: kSpiMode || kMySpiMode == at25040b :: kSpiModeAlternate , "the chip samples in SPI mode 0 or 3" ); static_assert ( kMyMsbFirst == at25040b :: kMsbFirst , "the chip takes MSB first" ); static_assert ( kMyCsGapNs >= at25040b :: BusTimingAt ( kMySupplyMv ). min_cs_high_ns , "CS high time below t_CS (Table 4-3)" ); class MyPort : public at25040b :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_spi_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One transfer, CS held low for all `len` bytes. `rx` is nullptr when no reply is needed. bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds: the driver polls the status every 100 us during a write. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Every hook is checked with its exact types and noexcept : a Transfer() with a uint16_t len , a DelayUs(uint16_t) or a hook without noexcept is a compile error, not a silent truncation. Bus requirements ¶ inc/at25040b_spi_interface.hpp states what the chip needs from the bus as constexpr values (datasheet "Features", section 4.3 Table 4-3, section 5). The scalar values hold over the whole supply range, 1.8 V to 5.5 V; BusTimingAt(supply_mv) returns the faster limits of a higher supply. Check your port's settings against them with static_assert , as the port above and the examples do. Constant Value Source kSpiMode , kSpiModeAlternate 0 (tested), 3 "Features": modes 0 and 3 kMsbFirst true Section 5, "MSB" kMaxClockHz 5 MHz; BusTimingAt() : 10 MHz from 2.5 V, 20 MHz from 4.5 V Table 4-3, f SCK kMinCsHighNs 200 ns; 100 ns from 2.5 V Table 4-3, t CS kCsSetupNs , kCsHoldNs 200 ns; 100 ns from 2.5 V Table 4-3, t CSS , t CSH kDataSetupNs , kDataHoldNs 80 ns; 40 ns from 2.5 V, 20 ns from 4.5 V Table 4-3, t SU , t H kContinuousWord false : idle SCK between bytes is fine, CS stays low Table 4-3 (no t WH /t WL maximum) kMaxTransferBytes 18: opcode, address, 16 data bytes The driver's read chunk Control pins ¶ Pin Polarity Idle level When the driver changes it WP ( CtrlPin::WriteProtect ) Active low: ACTIVE = pin low = writes blocked ACTIVE (low) Released ( INACTIVE , high) only for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, parked ACTIVE after CS Active low High (deselected) Never by the driver: the port's SPI controller drives it, low for each transfer. Drive it high before any device on the bus is clocked HOLD Active low High Never: tie it high (a HOLD strapped to CS makes every status read fail) The port drives WP to its idle level, low, before it enables the pin's output and before the first transfer (handbook KB-HW-018), so the chip never sees WP float high. For this pin the idle level is the asserted one: WP is a protection, and a glitch or a reset must leave the array protected. The driver never drives HOLD: tie it high. Transfer buffers ¶ The port only ever receives the driver's own two 18-byte transfer buffers, which are members of the driver object, never a caller's buffer or a stack array. If your SPI controller uses DMA, place the driver object in memory the DMA can reach (on ESP32, internal RAM, not a PSRAM task stack). Rules the transfer must follow: One call, one instruction. Keep CS low for all len bytes and raise it after: every instruction starts on a CS falling edge, and a write cycle starts when CS rises after the WRITE. Never split a transfer into several CS periods, and never join two. Mode 0 or 3, MSB first. At most BusTimingAt(supply_mv).max_clock_hz : 20 MHz from 4.5 V, 10 MHz from 2.5 V, 5 MHz from 1.8 V; start at 1 MHz on jumper wires. CS high for at least t CS between transfers. Raw bytes only. Do not interpret, retry or reorder bytes; the driver owns the framing and decides on retries. Return false for a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus (a pin hook into Error::Pin ) and never ignores it. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever. Shared bus. If other devices share the bus, take the bus lock in the port around each transfer, or in the handler around each driver call ( API guide ). Optional hooks ¶ The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with C++20 requires , in one place ( at25040b::detail ). A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way or fails to compile; it never skips a step silently. Hook Used for Without it GpioSet() WP: released for a write, a block-protection change and the identity check, parked after WP is the board's: tie it high for writes, or low for a read-only board (then Config::check_write_enable = false ) Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with every hook: class FullPort : public at25040b :: SpiInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_spi_init (); } bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_spi_transfer ( tx , rx , len ); } // Required: write cycles and status polls. void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: WP on a GPIO. ACTIVE means "protected", which is a low level on the pin. The driver // releases it only around writes and the identity check, and parks it after. bool GpioSet ( at25040b :: CtrlPin pin , at25040b :: GpioSignal signal ) noexcept { if ( pin != at25040b :: CtrlPin :: WriteProtect ) { return false ; } return platform_gpio_write ( kWpGpio , signal == at25040b :: GpioSignal :: INACTIVE ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( at25040b :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > at25040b :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } private : static constexpr int kWpGpio = 10 ; }; at25040b :: Error CheckWpWiring ( at25040b :: AT25040B < FullPort >& eeprom ) { // With the hook, EnsureInitialized() raises WP for WREN: a WP line that does not reach the chip // fails the start with DeviceIdMismatch, before any write is attempted. return eeprom . EnsureInitialized (). error ; } A GpioSet() that returns void , and a port without DelayUs() , are compile errors: the driver must see a failed pin write, and the write cycle wait is never skipped. The compile-fail tests check both rules. Reference implementations ¶ Every port lives with its example, in examples/<platform>/ ; the driver has none. Platforms lists them and how to add one. examples/host/host_at25040b_port.hpp : any PC, against a simulated chip. Start from it for a host build or a test bench; it is also the smallest complete port. examples/esp32/main/esp32_at25040b_port.hpp : ESP-IDF, with every hook. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Check your port ¶ Build it: the ports on this page are compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over them. Call EnsureInitialized() with the chip fitted: Ok proves that transfers work both ways, that CS frames each instruction and, with GpioSet() , that WP reaches the chip. GetLastStatusByte() is 0x00 on a new part. Unplug the chip (or lift CS) and call Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() : NoDevice or DeviceIdMismatch , never Ok . Write 16 bytes across a page boundary to an unused range and read them back. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several chips share a bus, the port or the handler must also serialise the bus. See Contract . Editor setup ¶ The clang-format and clang-tidy configuration is in _config/ , and the repository root has no copy of it. Tools that take a path use it directly; CI does the same: Tool Setting Command line clang-format --style=file:_config/.clang-format , clang-tidy --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy -p build VS Code (C/C++ extension) "C_Cpp.clang_format_style": "file:${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-format" and "C_Cpp.codeAnalysis.clangTidy.args": ["--config-file=${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-tidy"] clangd (VS Code clangd, Neovim, Emacs), CLion These find .clang-format and .clang-tidy only by name, from the file upwards: copy both to the root once ( cp _config/.clang-format _config/.clang-tidy . ). .gitignore lists the copies, so they never reach a commit; copy again after _config/ changes Configure with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (clangd: --compile-commands-dir=build ) so the editor sees the same flags as the build.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Run the driver on your PC first, with no hardware; then read the chip from your MCU: wire it, write a small port class, call two driver functions. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Microchip (Atmel) Atmel-8707 F: Pins and packages: 1 Pin Configurations, Table 1-1, p. 2 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Try it on your PC ¶ examples/host/ runs the real driver against a simulated AT25040B, through a host port. From the repository root, with CMake and a C++20 compiler: cmake -S examples/host -B build-example cmake --build build-example ./build-example/at25040b_host_example AT25040B driver 0.1.0 on the host at25040b: initialised wrote 12 bytes at 0x0FC in 2 write cycles read back: 6B 6F 6B 65 62 2D 61 74 32 35 00 01 at25040b: status reads 0xFF: nothing drives MISO after unplugging: NoDevice, status byte 0xFF The example checks the chip, writes 12 bytes across a page boundary (two write cycles), reads them back, then unplugs the simulated module and probes again. The calls in main.cpp are the ones below; only the port differs on an MCU. CI builds and runs this example on every pull request. 1. Wire it ¶ MCU AT25040B (SOIC-8, TSSOP-8) Notes SPI SCK SCK (pin 6) Mode 0 or 3; 1 MHz for bring-up on jumper wires SPI MOSI SI (pin 5) SPI MISO SO (pin 2) High impedance while CS is high, so the bus can be shared A GPIO or the SPI CS CS (pin 1) Low for one instruction, high between instructions A GPIO, or VCC WP (pin 3) Low blocks every write.
